summary:
Oyo State stands under the national framework of Nigeria, and that framework applies in full to visitors. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The statute reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, so attending a private ceremony is itself exposure.

Sexual conduct is separately criminal. Oyo is a southern state governed by the Criminal Code, which penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime. Twelve northern states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — apply Shari'a law, under which male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death.

Nigeria provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations themselves, so advocacy and support provision are criminal acts rather than safeguards.

Enforcement against individuals commonly proceeds through police profiling, entrapment and extortion of people perceived as gay, a practice known locally as "kito". Mass arrests recur across the country: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, and 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023.

Dating applications carry a documented abduction and extortion risk. An investigation broadcast on 15 May 2023 found criminal gangs posing as potential dates on popular apps, entraping men, filming them and then extorting, beating and kidnapping them; it interviewed 21 people who had been "kito'd". The same risk reaches gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria. Victims do not report these crimes to police, for fear of being arrested or assaulted themselves. The investigation also recorded police acting against the extortion gangs, including a commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of an officer detaining a suspect — enforcement directed at the blackmailers rather than their victims.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Country-wide mass arrests cut across the north-south legal divide. Kaduna, Gombe and the twelve Shari'a states sit in the north, while Lagos, Delta and Warri sit in the south under the Criminal Code, yet raid figures of dozens to more than a hundred detainees appear in both regions. Enforcement intensity in Oyo should be judged against that national pattern rather than against its own record.

The country's stated posture on dating-app extortion runs against the reporting behaviour of those targeted. Police units have publicly committed to pursuing blackmailers and have been filmed detaining suspects, while the people extorted avoid police contact entirely because a complaint exposes them to arrest under the same statutes the blackmailers invoke.

Foreign governments treat Nigeria as a heightened-risk destination on this axis. The UK travel advisory combines the national 14-year maximum with the death-penalty exposure in northern states, giving travellers a two-tier risk picture that changes materially if an itinerary crosses into the Shari'a zone.

Criminalisation coexists with visible public hostility rather than being confined to the statute book. Press coverage of the periods when prominent gender-nonconforming figures were in custody openly debated which prison section they should occupy, indicating that placement between male and female wings is left to administrative discretion.
localsOnly:
Residents of Oyo State live permanently under the SSMPA and the Criminal Code, with no anti-discrimination statute to appeal to in employment, housing, healthcare or policing. The 2014 Act's ban on registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations forecloses lawful collective representation, so there is no legally constituted body to lodge a complaint with.

Extortion by officers who allege same-sex conduct is an established method of extracting payments from people perceived as gay, and the local term for the practice, "kito", is in ordinary use for both the police variant and the criminal-gang variant.

Reporting is a documented trap. People approached through dating apps, filmed and blackmailed do not go to police, because the report itself evidences conduct punishable by up to 14 years and would expose them to arrest or assault.

Attendance at a same-sex ceremony is independently punishable under the SSMPA, so guests, organisers and assisting parties carry the same order of exposure as the couple.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Oyo-specific prosecution, raid, sentence or custody incident. Whether police in Oyo have conducted operations of the kind recorded in Lagos, Kaduna, Delta or Gombe is not sourced here, and the app-extortion reporting available describes a Lagos-based scene.

No source in this inventory addresses gender-marker or travel-document rules, access to facilities, access to hormone or other transition-related care, or recognition of partners for a trans visitor in Oyo. Those fields remain unresolved rather than answered in the negative.

Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here; Reuters reported the proposals in September 2022, and no later legislative outcome appears in this inventory.

The inventory supplies no count of anti-trans violence specific to Oyo State, and no data on how the Criminal Code's "gross indecency" provision has been applied to gender expression as opposed to sexual acts.
